newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl backs timely, stable European monetary union.
newsitem.headline: Kohl backs timely, stable European monetary union.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, addressing parliament after the European Union and Group of Seven summits, said on Friday that the EU Amsterdam treaty backed a timely start of a stable European monetary union.

"I am certain that we will introduce the euro according to plan -- punctually on January 1, 1999 and fully in line with the Maastricht criteria," he said in the text of a speech prepared for delivery in parliament.
"There was a clear signal from the summit in Amsterdam: the euro is coming," he said.

European economic and monetary union (EMU) was necessary in order to ensure that Europe, and particularly Germany, would be able to maintain its competitive position in the global economy, Kohl added.

In an apparent reference to increasing eurosceptic debate and calls in Germany to delay EMU, Kohl said: "Those who want to delay the introduction of the euro should know that this could possibly be a permanent delay. We cannot afford this."
Kohl added that were Europe to abandon the ambitious project to create a single currency, it would have severe consequences for jobs and exports in Germany and the continued integration of Europe.
"We would all pay dearly for the failure of the euro," he said, adding that there was broad consensus in Europe over the requirements for the euro and for lasting prosperity.

"We agree with the British and French governments, with all European partners, that price and budget stabilty together form the indispensible basis lasting (economic) growth and therefore more jobs," he said.
